docs.title: Connected Home
docs.text:
Welcome! This site documents the design, build, and day-to-day use of our Home Assistant-powered connected home.

  • For the Family - plain-language guides for using the smart home day to day.
  • Technical / Build Docs - detailed build notes, for Ryan or anyone rebuilding this from scratch.

This site is a work in progress

We're building this out iteratively, phase by phase. Check back as new sections are added.

docs.title: For the Family
docs.text:
This section will explain how to use the smart home day to day - things like:

  • Controlling lights, climate, and locks
  • What to do if something isn't responding
  • Who to ask (and what to check) before calling Ryan

Nothing lives here yet - this section gets filled in as each part of the house is built.

docs.title: Technical / Build Docs
docs.text:
Detailed build notes: what was installed, how it was configured, and why - written so a technically proficient person with the right access could rebuild this environment from scratch.

Architecture decisions are tracked as ADRs in the adr/ folder of the source repo, and will be surfaced here as the site grows.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
At a high level, the home network keeps smart-home/IoT devices on their own isolated network segment, separate from everyday devices and traffic. Home Assistant is reached remotely through Apple Home rather than by exposing it directly to the internet, using a Home Hub device already present in the house. The server running Home Assistant is treated as always-on infrastructure rather than general-purpose hardware.

Exact network addressing, hardware makes/models, and other build-identifying specifics are intentionally kept out of this public site - see the private repo's ADRs for the full reasoning.

docs.title: Deciding which network segment a device belongs on
docs.text:
Every device gets sorted into a segment using a hybrid of risk and function, rather than putting everything smart-home-related into one bucket. The general shape:

  • Trusted/primary - personal computing devices (laptops, phones, tablets) that hold or reach sensitive accounts and data.
  • General IoT - everyday smart-home convenience devices: speakers, hubs, sensors, thermostats, media players, and similar.
  • Security - anything that captures audio/video or controls physical access: cameras, locks, alarms, video doorbells/chimes, recorders. This gets its own segment, separate from general IoT, not folded into it - a compromised smart plug and a compromised camera are not the same kind of problem.
  • Guest - a separate concern from device classification, but the same isolation principle applies to visitor devices.

For any given device, the questions that decide its segment and its access rules:

  • Does it capture audio/video, or control physical entry? If so, it belongs in the most restricted segment, isolated from every other internal network, not just from the trusted one.
  • Does it need to be reachable from a phone app or from the home-automation hub? If so, that's a narrow, specific path to open - not a blanket opening between segments.
  • Does it need to discover other devices (e.g. via mDNS/SSDP)? Handle that with selective discovery-forwarding on the specific ports/services needed, rather than flattening segments back together for convenience.
  • What's its update/security track record? A device with no real firmware update history or a history of unpatched vulnerabilities is treated as higher risk regardless of what it does - and is a real candidate for replacement if it's meant to sit in a more trusted position.
  • If it were compromised, what could it reach next? Segments are designed so the answer is "as little as possible outside its own segment," not "everything on the same subnet."

The default access rule between segments: nothing is allowed to initiate a connection into a more trusted segment; a segment can receive return traffic for connections it initiated, and cross-device traffic within the same segment is denied by default unless a specific automation genuinely needs it.

Security-relevant devices (cameras, locks, alarms) aren't in the picture yet in this build. When they are, they're planned to land in a distinct, more restricted segment of their own rather than sharing the general IoT one - consistent with the reasoning above.

docs.title: Keeping services running without a login session
docs.text:
Background services on the host - including the virtual machine Home Assistant runs in - are managed as system-level background services rather than through their normal graphical applications, so everything keeps running without anyone being logged in. This was chosen deliberately over automatic login, which would have compromised another feature of the host machine we wanted to keep.

Two habits fall out of that choice, worth knowing if you're maintaining a setup like this: don't start something through its graphical application at the same time its background-service equivalent is managing it - they'll conflict over the same underlying files. And stopping the background service isn't the same as shutting the thing it's running down cleanly - always shut down the guest/service itself first, then stop the background service around it.

Exact service names, file paths, and configuration are intentionally kept out of this public site - see the private repo's ADRs for the full rebuild-from-scratch detail.

docs.title: Cataloguing existing devices
docs.text:
Rather than typing up the device inventory by hand, the starting point is generated programmatically: a small script queries the network controller's official local API for every currently connected client and network device, and exports that into a spreadsheet as a base list - name, address, wired vs. wireless, last seen, and so on. That raw export is then hand-annotated with what the API can't know on its own: whether a device has native Home Assistant support, whether it depends on a vendor cloud service to function, which network segment it belongs on (see above), who in the household uses it, and so on.

The exact API endpoints, credentials, and the script itself live in the private repo, not here - see its inventory tooling for the source of truth.

docs.title: Naming, automation, and access principles
docs.text:
Before any devices are wired into Home Assistant, a small set of house rules governs how they'll be named, how automations get built, and who gets what level of access - so these don't need retrofitting later as the system grows.

Naming follows an area-first pattern: friendly names read naturally ("Living Room Lamp," not a vendor-generated identifier), and the underlying technical IDs are built the same way (domain, then area, then device), so both the dashboard and voice control stay predictable as more devices are added. People in the household who refer to a space differently than its official name (e.g. calling a room by a nickname) get that covered by an alias rather than a rename.

Automations are kept thin: something that decides when an action should happen (the automation) calls into something that performs the action (a script for a sequence, a scene for an instant state) rather than mixing the two together. Anything that changes a device's physical state is expected to define what "safe" looks like if a step fails partway through, rather than leaving things in an unclear state. Local integrations are preferred over cloud-dependent ones where both exist, and anything that matters for daily life gets a manual way to override it that doesn't require understanding the underlying automation.

Access follows a simple, deliberately conservative default: administrator rights are granted per person, not handed out automatically just because someone lives in the house, and every household member who wants day-to-day control gets their own account and dashboard rather than sharing one login. Visitor access is handled outside Home Assistant entirely, through the same remote-access path already in place for the household.

Nothing else lives here yet beyond this overview - filled in phase by phase.
